implementation_notes: Ruby keeps the storage on the Thread object itself: Thread.current.thread_variable_set(key, value) and thread_variable_get(key) address a hash that belongs to the thread and is carried across fibers, which the documentation distinguishes explicitly from the bracket API. The classic key/collection/proxy structure is replaced by the Thread instance - no key is allocated, no destructor exists, and entries persist for the thread's lifetime. Choose this form when all fibers of a thread must share the value; choose the bracket form below when the isolation unit should be the fiber (the usual case for per-request state under a fiber scheduler). Values are never inherited by new threads, so a worker that needs them must set them.
pitfalls: The bracket API (Thread#[] and Thread#[]=) looks like the same thing but is fiber-local; the documentation states the difference and points thread-local users at thread_variable_get/set.
New threads inherit nothing, so a thread pool must set the value in the worker body or the accessor returns nil.
There is no thread-exit cleanup for user keys: pooled or long-lived threads keep the referenced objects alive until the key is cleared.
Keys are symbols (strings are converted with to_sym), and the same name used through thread_variable_set and []= yields two independent slots.

variants.name: Thread#[] / Thread#[]= (fiber-local storage)
variants.implementation_notes: The bracket API is what most Ruby code actually uses for per-request state, and the documentation is explicit that it is fiber-local: each fiber has its own bucket, so under a fiber-based server every request runs in its own fiber and gets clean isolation with no cleanup at all, while code that sets a value and then creates a Fiber (or uses an Enumerator, which is a fiber) sees nil inside. Use it deliberately as fiber-local storage - Ruby's per-execution-context solution - and switch to thread_variable_get/set only when all fibers of a thread must share one value. Neither API provides a cleanup hook.
variants.code_sketch:
Thread.current[:request_id] = request.id     # FIBER-local: a fresh fiber sees nil

def request_id = Thread.current[:request_id]

Fiber.new { request_id }.resume               # nil - its own bucket
pitfalls: The name suggests thread scope while the semantics are fiber scope - the most common misuse of the API.
Fiber-scheduler libraries move work between fibers, so a fiber-local value can disappear mid-request unless the framework re-establishes it.
Bracket keys and thread_variable keys are independent even when the name matches, so mixing the two APIs silently loses values.
